india.headline: Cyclone Akvan hits land near Gopalpur, weaker than feared
india.summary: Cyclone Akvan has reached land. The weather office (IMD) says it crossed the coast near Gopalpur in Odisha between 7:30 and 8:30 this morning, with winds of 70–80 km/h gusting to 90. That is gentler than Thursday's forecast of 90–100 km/h, because the storm weakened overnight. Odisha had already moved about 3 lakh people into 2,523 relief camps.
india.why: Over warm water a cyclone keeps refuelling. Once it drifts over land, that fuel is cut off, so it slowly loses strength. Rain, however, keeps falling for hours, and Akvan is the third storm to threaten this coast in 24 days.
india.soWhat: Heavy rain can continue in south Odisha and north Andhra. Railways have cancelled dozens of trains, so check before travelling.
india.take: Weaker winds are good news, but flooding often does the real damage.
india.watch: IMD rainfall warnings for Ganjam and Puri, and when trains resume.

world.soWhat: A real ceasefire would ease pressure on oil and fertiliser prices that Indian households and farmers feel.

world.headline: Japan's prices rise faster as energy help ends, rate hike likely
world.summary: Prices in Japan rose 2.3% in October from a year earlier, up from 2.1% in September, government data showed on Friday. Core inflation, which leaves out fresh food, rose to 2.2%. world.soWhat: Higher Japanese rates can pull money out of riskier markets like India's and make yen loans to Indian firms costlier.
world.take: Japan's inflation now looks home-grown, not just imported, so higher rates are overdue.

world.headline: Climate talks drop fossil fuel exit from draft deal on final day
world.summary: At the UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, a new draft deal released on Thursday removed every mention of fossil fuels. An earlier version had called for a faster phase-out of coal, oil and gas. The nine-page text instead backs raising electricity's share of world energy use to 35% by 2035, from about 20% today. Talks are due to end Friday but may run longer.
world.why: Nearly 200 countries must all agree, so one holdout can block a deal. Panama threatens to veto anything weak. Money shrank too: a target of at least $120 billion a year for adaptation was removed, though poorer nations need about $305 billion annually by 2035.
world.soWhat: India opposes making the electricity goal binding, and Indian farmers and coastal cities need the adaptation money now left vague.
world.take: A climate deal that cannot name fossil fuels is ducking the main problem.

investing.soWhat: Today you pay about ₹19 for each rupee of yearly profit (its P/E). Buyers usually paid about ₹46. So it's far cheaper than its own normal.
investing.take: A cash-rich, debt-free leader priced as if growth has ended.

psychology.label: Psychology · 20 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Why a longer painful experience can be remembered as better
psychology.summary: In a 1993 experiment, 32 male students put one hand in painfully cold water for 60 seconds. With the other hand they did the same, then stayed in 30 seconds more while the water warmed slightly. Asked which trial to repeat, 22 of 32, about 69%, chose the longer one. They picked more total pain because it ended better.
psychology.why: Daniel Kahneman and colleagues called it the peak-end rule. When we look back on an experience, memory leans on its worst moment and its final moment. How long it lasted barely counts, which they called duration neglect.
psychology.soWhat: Your memory of a trip, a doctor's visit or a meeting is shaped mostly by its worst moment and how it finished.
psychology.take: How something ends deserves more planning than how long it runs.
psychology.watch: Notice which moments you mention first when describing your last holiday.

terms.meaning: Memory judges experiences by worst and final moments

psychology.example: A long wedding is remembered for the late-night dancing, not the two-hour wait for dinner.
psychology.useThisWeek: End one meeting or family outing on a deliberately pleasant note, then ask people how it went.

psychology.label: Psychology · 20 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: A small yes today makes a big yes more likely later
psychology.summary: In 1966, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser asked residents of Palo Alto, California, to put a very large 'Drive Carefully' sign on their front lawn. Only 16.7% of people asked cold agreed. But 76% agreed if they had earlier said yes to a tiny three-inch safe-driving sign. The small request opened the door.
psychology.why: This is the foot-in-the-door technique. The researchers suggested that agreeing once changes how people see themselves: as someone who backs causes like this. Even a different first favour, like signing a petition, roughly lifted agreement to about 47%.
psychology.soWhat: Salespeople, apps and fundraisers often start with a tiny ask. Spot the pattern before a small yes commits you to more.
psychology.take: Small commitments are worth guarding because they quietly shape who we think we are.
psychology.watch: Count how many small sign-up steps come before the paid plan this week.

terms.meaning: Small request first to win a bigger one

sources.label: Freedman and Fraser (1966), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

study.authors: Jonathan L. Freedman and Scott C. Fraser

psychology.example: A colleague asks you to check one slide, then later asks you to present the whole deck.
psychology.useThisWeek: Before agreeing to any 'quick favour', ask yourself whether you would also say yes to the bigger request that may follow.

psychology.label: Psychology · 20 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Most people obey a pointless rule even when nobody checks
psychology.summary: Picture an empty road at night and a red light. Do you wait? A 2025 study with 14,034 online participants tested this. In a game, waiting at a red light cost money, nobody watched, and breaking the rule hurt no one. Still, 55–70% waited. Seeing one other player jump the light cut waiting by about eight percentage points.
psychology.why: Economists Simon Gächter, Lucas Molleman and Daniele Nosenzo argue that many people respect rules for their own sake, and expect others to as well. Fines and kindness to others mattered less. The tests used US online workers and Nottingham students, so results may differ elsewhere.
psychology.soWhat: One visible rule-breaker in a queue, office or housing society can quickly make cutting corners feel normal for everyone.
psychology.take: Showing that most people follow a rule may work better than threatening fines.
psychology.watch: Notice what happens to a queue after the first person cuts in.

terms.meaning: Simple difference between two percentages

study.authors: Simon Gächter, Lucas Molleman and Daniele Nosenzo

psychology.example: At a deserted signal at midnight, many drivers still wait for green with no traffic police in sight.
psychology.useThisWeek: If you manage a team or a society group, remind people how many already follow a rule instead of only warning about penalties.

psychology.label: Psychology · 20 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: A small blunder can make a capable person more likeable
psychology.summary: In 1966, Elliot Aronson and colleagues played 48 male University of Minnesota students a taped quiz interview. One candidate answered 92% of questions right; another got 30%. On some tapes the candidate then spilled coffee all over his new suit. The star who spilled was liked most, scoring 30.2. The average candidate who spilled was liked least, at -2.5.
psychology.why: The researchers called it a humanising effect, now known as the pratfall effect. Someone who seems flawless can feel distant and unapproachable. A harmless slip makes them seem human. But the same slip only confirms doubts about someone who has not yet shown skill.
psychology.soWhat: If people already trust your work, admitting a small mistake can help. If they don't, prove your ability first.
psychology.take: Competence earns you the right to be clumsy.
psychology.watch: Notice how colleagues react when a senior leader admits a minor error.

terms.meaning: A skilled person's blunder raises their likeability

sources.label: Aronson, Willerman and Floyd (1966), Psychonomic Science (Springer)

study.authors: Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman and Joanne Floyd

psychology.example: A top teacher who laughs after misspelling a word on the board often seems warmer to the class.
psychology.useThisWeek: In your next presentation, own up to one small slip lightly instead of hiding it, and see how the room responds.

psychology.label: Psychology · 20 Nov 2026
psychology.headline: Follow-up questions help strangers feel connected in conversation
psychology.summary: What makes a chat with a stranger click? A study published in November 2025 recorded 646 people in two experiments talking to someone new. In a 10-minute deep conversation, people who asked more follow-up questions and said things like 'that makes sense' left partners feeling more connected. A short coaching exercise raised follow-up questions by 23%.
psychology.why: Researchers led by Taylor West and Barbara Fredrickson at the University of North Carolina wanted proof of what good listening looks like. In brief small talk, overall attentiveness mattered more than question counts. Most volunteers were women from one university, which limits the findings.
psychology.soWhat: At a new job, a family function or a networking event, a well-placed follow-up question builds more warmth than a clever story.
psychology.take: Good listening is a skill you can practise, not a personality trait.
psychology.watch: Count your follow-up questions in your next conversation with someone new.

terms.meaning: Questions building on what the other person said

sources.label: West, Huston, Chandler, Zhou and Fredrickson (2025), Communications Psychology

study.authors: Taylor N. West, Sara Huston, Kylie R. Chandler, Jieni Zhou and Barbara L. Fredrickson

psychology.example: When a new colleague mentions they moved from Pune, asking 'What do you miss most?' beats jumping to your own Pune story.
psychology.useThisWeek: In two conversations this week, ask at least two follow-up questions before sharing anything about yourself.
